summary: Describes why the SIP 503 response is not enough for handling overload, when proxies and user agents lack resources to process requests, and lists requirements for a better mechanism. This is an informational document.

eli5.summary: When a shop gets too crowded, just saying come back later does not work well, because everyone returns at once. This memo lists what a better way of handling the crowd should do.

questions: why sip 503 response is not enough
subtitle: Fixing SIP when servers get too busy.

tldr.problem: SIP networks need ways to handle overload when proxies and servers lack resources to process requests. The existing 503 response mechanism has serious problems that make overload worse.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5390 identifies why the 503 mechanism fails (load amplification, underutilization, oscillation, ambiguity) and sets out 23 requirements for a better overload control solution.
tldr.outcome: The requirements guide future SIP protocol development to prevent overload from cascading through networks and to maintain throughput during heavy traffic.

facts.label: Worst-case amplification
facts.value: Single request generates up to 18 messages

today: RFC 5390 established the foundational requirements that have guided SIP overload control solutions. The IETF's SIP Overload Control Working Group (which operated circa 2009-2012) produced RFC 6357 (Clarifications on the Use of RTCP in RTP Sessions) and related work on SIP-specific overload mechanisms. The requirements for graded throttling and mixed deployment remain central to modern SIP capacity planning. The mechanism RFC 5390 calls for has informed both standardized solutions and operational practices in large SIP networks.

sections.title: SIP Overload and the 503 Problem
sections.content:
Overload occurs in SIP networks when proxies and user agents lack sufficient resources—CPU, memory, I/O, disk, or external services like databases—to process incoming requests. When overloaded, a server can respond with a 503 (Service Unavailable) response code and optionally include a Retry-After header indicating how long upstream elements should wait before retrying.

In theory, this allows work to be redirected to other servers and gives the overloaded server time to clear its backlog. In practice, the mechanism has severe problems. This RFC describes why the 503 mechanism fails in real deployments and establishes requirements for a better approach.
sections.eli5: When a SIP server gets too busy, it can say "come back later." The problem is that this doesn't actually help, and can make things worse.

sections.title: Sources of Overload
sections.content:
Overload can arise from many sources. Poor capacity planning causes a network to be built without enough capacity for normal and predictable peak loads (such as high calling volumes on Mother's Day). Dependency failures occur when a critical external resource, like a database or DNS server, fails or becomes slow, even though the SIP element itself has capacity. Component failures in a cluster reduce capacity when one or more servers fail and others absorb their load. Capacity planning usually accounts for this, but unusual failures can exceed reserves.

Avalanche restart is particularly problematic. When many clients simultaneously connect (such as after a power outage in a city, when all phones reboot and register; or when a network connection is restored, or when clients detect a failed proxy and reconnect), the server receives a flood of registration requests in a short time. With UDP and retransmissions, this can multiply the load sevenfold.

Other sources include flash crowds (an advertisement directs many users to call a number simultaneously) and denial-of-service attacks. Overload tends to compound: when servers are overloaded, they slow down, causing more retransmissions, which increases load further. With up to seven UDP retransmits per INVITE before timeout, a single incoming request can generate 18 requests and responses in the network.
sections.eli5: Servers get overloaded for different reasons: too many customers planned for, a database that got slow, one server crashing so another takes all the work, everyone powering back on at once, a TV ad directing millions of calls to one number, or an attack. Each makes the network busier.

sections.title: Why 503 Makes Overload Worse
sections.content:
The 503 mechanism has four critical flaws:

Load Amplification: When servers are overloaded and a proxy receives 503s, it retries the request on other servers. Those servers are also overloaded, so they also send 503s. The same request gets tried on server S1, then S2, then S3, each involving retransmissions. A single client request can generate 18 or more request-response pairs under UDP before timing out, using up precious resources of overloaded servers. With cascading proxies, this amplification worsens further. The mechanism works for isolated overloaded elements, but fails when the network itself is overloaded.

Underutilization: When a hostname maps to a cluster of servers via DNS SRV records, many implementations interpret a 503 from one server to mean the entire cluster is overloaded. They stop sending traffic to all servers in the cluster, even if some are underutilized. This reduces overall network capacity precisely when it is needed most.

Oscillation: The Retry-After mechanism is all-or-nothing: a server either turns off all traffic or none. When two servers share load and one sends Retry-After, all traffic moves to the second server, overloading it. When it also sends Retry-After, all traffic waits and then floods back to the first server when the timer expires. This creates highly oscillatory behavior and unstable load distribution.

Ambiguous Usages: The 503 response is used for many purposes beyond overload, such as when a gateway receives certain failure codes from downstream systems that have nothing to do with the gateway's own capacity. This makes it hard for upstream elements to know whether retrying on another server will help or whether the problem is shared across multiple servers.
sections.eli5: The 503 response has four problems: (1) trying another server just multiplies work on all servers, (2) one server rejecting can block the whole cluster, (3) blocking and unblocking at once causes swings between overloaded and underutilized, and (4) 503 is used for things that have nothing to do with overload, so you don't know if retrying will help.

sections.title: Requirements for Better Overload Control
sections.content:
RFC 5390 proposes 23 requirements for an improved overload mechanism:

Fundamental Performance: The mechanism must maintain useful throughput even when incoming load far exceeds capacity, prioritizing overall system value (REQ 1). It must limit the impact of individual element failures to prevent cascade effects (REQ 2).

Signaling: Overload signals must explicitly indicate overload rather than other failures, avoiding ambiguity (REQ 6). The mechanism must handle cases where elements fail completely and cannot send any signal (REQ 15). It should minimize messaging overhead (REQ 16) and be unambiguous about whether load applies to an IP address, hostname, or URI (REQ 18).

Throttling: Unlike 503's all-or-nothing approach, the mechanism must provide graded throttling (REQ 7) allowing partial reduction of traffic to reflect degrees of overload. Rejected requests must not be retried on overloaded elements whose status is unknown (REQ 8), and rejection from one element must not prevent submission to unloaded elements (REQ 9).

Deployment: The mechanism must work with mixed environments of supporting and non-supporting elements with incremental improvement (REQ 4) and must work across domain boundaries (REQ 12). It must not require extensive configuration (REQ 3) and must properly handle load balancers and both enumerable and non-enumerable upstream elements (REQ 10, 11, 23).

Fairness and Security: It should work in untrusted environments, preventing malicious elements from hogging resources (REQ 5). Operators must be able to restrict load reporting by source (REQ 22). In mixed environments, no disproportionate benefit should accrue to non-implementing elements (REQ 20).

Routing and Priority: Local overload policies must be respected, allowing emergency calls or high-priority messages preferential treatment (REQ 13). Clients need clear guidance on when to retry, especially for TCP connections and registrations to prevent avalanche restart (REQ 14). The mechanism must be stable: when offered load drops below capacity, throughput should stabilize (REQ 21).
sections.eli5: A better mechanism should: handle high load without falling apart, tell the truth about why it's rejecting, let you reduce traffic gradually not all at once, work with mixed old and new systems, be fair to everyone, let you prioritize emergency calls, and prevent everyone from reconnecting at the same moment.

sections.title: Security and Stability
sections.content:
Overload handling must prevent both outside attacks (such as denial-of-service flooding) and inside attacks from untrusted elements. Any overload signaling mechanism creates potential attack surfaces: a malicious element could claim overload falsely to starve competitors of traffic, or could ignore overload signals to gain unfair advantage.

The requirement that the mechanism work without explicit signals (when elements fail completely) means the system must function even when communication itself is compromised. The requirement that it work in untrusted environments means it must prevent malicious elements from gaming the system.

On the stability side, an overload mechanism is only valuable if it actually improves network behavior. It must prevent oscillation (rapidly switching between accepting and rejecting), maintain fairness (not allowing well-behaved elements to starve), and degrade gracefully as network load increases and then decreases.
sections.eli5: Someone might lie about being overloaded to block competitors, or ignore signals to cheat. The system has to work even when you can't talk to a server, and has to stay stable—not swinging wildly between accepting and rejecting requests.
